paras: On the other hand, you may need very little more support. Start small—do shorter practices, make them warm, choose a small and tractable subject to work with, make sure you’re coming all the way back out of hypnosis, and track the effect on one target area (anxiety, daydreaming, repairing a relationship, an avoided task, sleep, emotional regulation, intuitive accuracy, etc.) for a week or two. If you find that your functioning worsens or you’re gaining certainty about memories that can’t be verified, then it’s time to reassess, not to push harder.

paras: Methods to explore with a trained person present

If you want to do deliberate trauma-focused regression, to follow an affect or somatic bridge to unknown traumatic origins, or to work with substantial flashbacks or dissociative reactions, work with a trauma-informed trained clinician who is trained in the method you’re using and who is present while you do it. (Affect and somatic bridges mean following associations from an emotional or bodily feeling; regression means remembering or imagining what it would have been like when you were younger. Both can have other uses too, like finding resources.) Ask what they intend to do and how they’ll handle uncertainty and unexpected reactions. Even if you work with a clinician, please note that hypnosis can’t prove what did or didn’t happen in your life.

paras: The ultimate feedback on whether your process is working well is how you’re functioning in ordinary life. If you’re being more loving, honest, functional, relational, grounded, and precise than you were before you started, then keep going, gently. If ordinary life is getting less stable, then stop trying to go deeper and focus instead on getting enough sleep, eating, grounding yourself, maintaining healthy boundaries with others, and getting support from others.
